title: TCP Fast Open
summary: This experimental document describes TCP Fast Open, which allows data in SYN and SYN-ACK packets, consumed during the handshake, saving up to one round trip. TFO deviates from standard TCP behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP Fast Open lets a client send its first data with the packet that starts a TCP connection. A server can act on that data before the usual handshake finishes, but an application must be able to handle a replay of the data.

questions: how to send data in syn
how does tcp fast open work
subtitle: Put a returning client's first data in the TCP handshake to save a round trip.

tldr.problem: Ordinary TCP waits for its three-way handshake to finish before delivering data, adding a round trip before an application can act on the first request.
tldr.mechanism: A server gives a client a Fast Open cookie. On a later connection, the client sends the cookie and data in its SYN, and a server that accepts the cookie can deliver the data before the handshake ends.
tldr.outcome: TCP Fast Open can save up to one round-trip time, but the data in a SYN can be replayed in rare cases. RFC 7413 is Experimental.

today: RFC 7413 is an Experimental RFC published in December 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC warns that SYN data may be replayed and says applications should use TFO only when they can tolerate that risk.

sections.title: Data Before the Handshake Ends
sections.content:
Ordinary Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) uses a three-way handshake before the receiver delivers data to an application. TCP Fast Open (TFO) relaxes that rule so a server can deliver data carried in a SYN, potentially saving one round-trip time.

This changes TCP behavior: an old or duplicate SYN may reach the application again after the server has forgotten the first one. A spoofed SYN could also make the server spend resources processing data before the handshake completes. For these reasons, TCP implementations must not enable TFO by default; an application must request it for a service port.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP Fast Open lets a server receive application data before a connection is fully established. The same data may be delivered again in rare cases, so applications must be able to tolerate duplicates.

sections.title: Cookies and the Fast Open Exchange
sections.content:
The server creates a Fast Open cookie, a message authentication code that authenticates the client's source IP address. The client first requests a cookie in a SYN with an empty cookie field; the server returns one in its SYN-ACK, and the client saves it.

On a later connection, the client sends data and the cookie in its SYN. If the cookie is valid, the server acknowledges the data and delivers it to the application. If not, the server acknowledges only the SYN; the client can retransmit unacknowledged data in its next ACK and continue with ordinary TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first asks the server for a cookie and saves the server's reply. Later it sends that cookie with its first data, and the server delivers the data only if the cookie is valid.

sections.title: The TCP Fast Open Option
sections.content:
The Fast Open TCP option has Kind value 34. Its Length is an even number from 6 to 18 bytes, and the cookie is either empty or 4 to 16 bytes long. An empty cookie requests one from the server; a present cookie is sent back to perform Fast Open.

The client must cache cookies by client and server IP address, and the RFC recommends caching the server's Maximum Segment Size. Without a cached value, SYN data is limited to the default MSS of 536 bytes for IPv4 or 1220 bytes for IPv6. The client also records negative responses and should temporarily disable TFO on a path that fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries either an empty cookie request or a cookie supplied by the server. If the client has not saved the server's maximum segment size, the RFC gives default data limits for IPv4 and IPv6.

sections.title: Replay, Spoofing and Applicability
sections.content:
A client must not send SYN data with TFO if it cannot handle that data being received more than once. A server must not accept SYN data if its application cannot handle duplicates. The cookie helps prevent spoofed SYNs from triggering application work, but valid cookies do not remove every resource-exhaustion or reflection risk.

The server keeps a limit on pending Fast Open requests and disables TFO for new requests while that limit is exceeded. A small first request can benefit most; the RFC gives HTTP GET as a suitable example and warns against replay-sensitive POST requests without application protection. It also says a TLS client hello can be sent in the SYN.
sections.plainLanguage: Use Fast Open only when repeating the first request would be safe. Servers also limit pending requests, because a valid cookie does not prevent every attack.
